title: Halal food today
hookLine: certification, supply chains, and the spirit of tayyib

cards: A small logo in the corner of a package of chicken: a crescent, maybe, or Arabic letters, and an organization you've never heard of.
Behind it is a whole chain: a farm, a slaughterhouse, a factory, a truck, a freezer, an inspector with a clipboard. A shopper glances at it for half a second.
But the verse behind the logo has a second word, and it never fits on a label.

teach.b: Here's the verse, from Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall: "O mankind! Eat of that which is lawful and wholesome in the earth." It's addressed to mankind, everyone at the table. And there are two words, not one.
Lawful is halal: what's permitted. The Qur'an names what isn't, in Surah al-Ma'idah: carrion, blood, pork, and meat dedicated to anything other than Allah. Wholesome is tayyib: good, pure, pleasant.
Halal is a line. Tayyib is a quality. Now the modern part.

teach.h: HALAL IS A LINE. TAYYIB IS A QUALITY.
teach.b: A certifying body checks the halal side: how the animal was slaughtered, whether a gelatin came from pork, whether a flavoring hides alcohol, whether the halal meat touched other meat on the line. That's real work.
Certifiers and scholars don't all agree on the details, like whether an animal may be stunned before slaughter, or whether a machine may do the cutting.

And some Muslims read another verse in al-Ma'idah, that the food of the People of the Book is lawful, as covering meat from Jews and Christians today, while others don't. Then the second word asks more than any stamp.

In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that Allah has prescribed excellence in everything, and that when you slaughter, you should do it well: sharpen the blade, and spare the animal suffering.
Some Muslims hear tayyib in that, reaching back up the chain to how the animal lived and died; some now ask the same of the workers and the land.

teach.h: SHARPEN THE BLADE, SPARE THE ANIMAL.
teach.b: The logo can say halal. Only the whole chain can say good.

how: Muslims who keep halal often look for certification marks on meat and packaged food, check ingredient lists for things like pork gelatin or alcohol, and differ among themselves on questions such as stunning and the meat of the People of the Book.

o: food sold only in Muslim shops, under one world authority
any food a Muslim has blessed by saying a prayer over it
food checked as lawful, with tayyib asking that it be good too

games.q: lawful and good — tap the pairs.
p: sharpen the blade, spare the animal

s: the verse on lawful and wholesome food is addressed only to Muslims
halal and tayyib mean exactly the same thing
halal is what's permitted; tayyib is wholesome, good, pure.
certifiers and scholars differ on whether stunning before slaughter is allowed
it's one of the live debates in halal food today.

games.q: you're a butcher, and you've got an animal to slaughter. according to the hadith in Sahih Muslim, what's asked of you?
o: just say the right words; the rest doesn't matter.
do it well: sharpen the blade, spare the animal suffering.
do it quickly, however it's done.
games.why: the hadith says Allah has prescribed excellence in everything: sharpen the blade, and spare the animal. the law and the kindness come in one breath.

practice: Bring the last thing you ate to mind and trace it backward: who sold it, who carried it, who made it, where it grew or how it lived. You won't know most of the answers; just notice how long the chain is.
If you pray, hold the two words together, lawful and wholesome, and give thanks as you usually do; if you don't, thank one link in the chain.

wordCard.voice: Halal food today. Food checked as lawful, from a certifier's stamp all the way back to the farm, with tayyib, wholesome and good, asking for more. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: good, wholesome, pure; the word paired with halal in 2:168.

carryVoice: Your line: lawful and good. Halal is the line; tayyib asks for more. I'll be here tomorrow.
